title: Dictionaries
summary: A dictionary stores values under named keys. Each key helps you look up one value.
introduction: A dictionary stores values under named keys. Each key helps you look up one value. Think of a word book: a word is the key, and its meaning is the value. Make a small record and look up a fact by its key.
learningObjectives: Create dictionaries and read, add, update and delete entries
Handle missing keys with in, get() and setdefault()
Loop over keys, values and items
Build and navigate nested structures of dicts and lists

blocks.title: basics.py
blocks.code:
user = {"name": "Ada", "age": 36, "languages": ["Python", "SQL"]}

print(user["name"])
print(user["languages"][0])
print(len(user))

user["age"] = 37                    # update an existing key
user["email"] = "ada@example.com"   # add a new key
del user["languages"]               # remove a key
print(user)
print("email" in user, "languages" in user)

blocks.text: Curly braces with `key: value` pairs create a dictionary. Keys are usually strings but can be any immutable value (numbers, tuples); values can be anything, including lists and other dictionaries. Entries keep the order in which they were inserted, so printing a dictionary shows it as you built it. The `in` operator tests *keys*, not values.

blocks.title: python missing.py
blocks.content:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/ada/projects/missing.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(stock["banana"])
          ~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^
KeyError: 'banana'

blocks.text: Indexing a key that does not exist raises `KeyError`. That is right when the key *must* exist (a bug should be loud) and wrong when the key legitimately might not. Three tools cover the second case: `in` to test first, `get()` to read with a default, and `setdefault()` to insert a default only when the key is absent.

blocks.title: safe.py
blocks.code:
stock = {"apple": 5, "pear": 0}

print(stock.get("banana"))
print(stock.get("banana", 0))
print(stock.get("apple", 0))

if "pear" in stock:
    print("We stock pears:", stock["pear"])

stock.setdefault("banana", 12)   # add only if missing
stock.setdefault("apple", 99)    # apple exists: unchanged
print(stock)
print(stock.pop("pear"), stock.pop("kiwi", "none"))
print(stock)

blocks.text: `get()` without a default returns `None` for a missing key, which is fine for a quick check but easy to pass along by accident; give it an explicit default whenever the value is used in a calculation. `pop(key, default)` removes an entry and returns its value, with the same default mechanism.

blocks.text: Looping over a dictionary yields its keys. `items()` gives `(key, value)` pairs, which is what you want most of the time; `keys()` and `values()` give live views of one side that you can pass to `list()`, `sum()` or `sorted()`. `max(prices, key=prices.get)` finds the key with the largest value, a one-liner you will reuse constantly.

blocks.title: counting.py
blocks.code:
from collections import Counter

text = "the cat and the dog and the bird"
counts = {}
for word in text.split():
    counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1
print(counts)

counter = Counter(text.split())
print(counter.most_common(2))

blocks.text: `counts.get(word, 0) + 1` is *the* counting idiom: read the current count (zero if the word is new), add one, store it back. The standard library's `Counter` packages the same idea and adds helpers such as `most_common()`.

blocks.title: Changing a dictionary while looping over it
blocks.text: Adding or removing keys inside `for key in my_dict:` raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`. Loop over a snapshot of the keys instead, `for key in list(my_dict):`, or build a new dictionary containing only the entries you want to keep.
A dictionary of lists of dictionaries is exactly how JSON APIs deliver data. Read a path such as `library["books"][1]["title"]` left to right: the library, its books, the second one, its title.

questions.question: `prices.___("tea", 0)` returns the value stored under `"tea"`, or `0` if the key is missing, without raising an error.
questions.explanation: `get(key, default)` is the safe read. `setdefault()` would also insert the key, and plain indexing raises `KeyError`.

questions.question: A Python dictionary remembers the order in which its keys were inserted.
questions.explanation: Since Python 3.7, dictionaries preserve insertion order, so looping and printing show entries in the order you added them.
